chunks: Leave me and seek someone else.
For we are facing a matter which has (several) faces and colours, which neither hearts can stand nor intelligence can accept. Clouds are hovering over the sky, and faces are not discernable.
You should know that if I respond to you I would lead you as I know and would not care about whatever one may say or abuse.
If you leave me then I am the same as you are. It is possible I would listen to and obey whomever you make in charge of your affairs. I am better for you as a counsellor than as a chief!

key_terms.الْآفَاقَ: the horizons/sky (metaphor for the general situation)
key_terms.الْمَحَجَّةَ: the path/way (metaphor for clarity of direction)
key_terms.وُجُوهٌ وَأَلْوَانٌ: faces and colours (metaphor for complexity and varying aspects)

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali suggest leaving him to seek another leader after Uthman's murder?
ai.summary: This famous hadith, known as 'Hadith al-Tamassuk' or the 'Offer of Caliphate,' reflects Imam Ali’s (AS) strategic humility and political realism during the volatile post-Uthman era, where tribal rivalries threatened to fracture the Muslim community. By offering to serve as a minister rather than assume the caliphate, he prioritized communal stability and the acceptance of the people over personal authority, a stance deeply analyzed in Shia jurisprudence regarding the conditions of leadership (Imamah). This moment highlights the tension between divine knowledge and political expediency, a theme central to the Nahj al-Balagha's portrayal of his governance.
